summary: Specifies security mechanisms for the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP), which is vulnerable to attacks if unsecured. Unlike the original specifications, SEND does not use IPsec.

eli5.summary: Computers on a local network ask each other who is who. SEND adds proof so a liar cannot pretend to be someone else.

questions: how to secure ipv6 neighbor discovery
what is a cryptographically generated address
how does send stop replay attacks
what icmpv6 types does send use
subtitle: How IPv6 neighbors and routers prove who they are on a local link, using signatures instead of IPsec.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery lets any node on a link claim an address or pose as a router, and the original answer of protecting it with IPsec needed manual security associations that were impractical.
tldr.mechanism: SEND adds new Neighbor Discovery options: a CGA option proving address ownership, an RSA Signature option over the message, Timestamp and Nonce options against replay, and certification paths that let hosts check a router against a trust anchor.
tldr.outcome: Secured and unsecured Neighbor Discovery can coexist on a link, with secured information taking priority. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 6494, RFC 6495 and RFC 6980.

today: RFC 3971 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6494, RFC 6495 and RFC 6980, which should be read alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with Unsecured Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
IPv6 nodes use the Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) to find each other on a link, learn link-layer addresses, find routers and track whether neighbors are still reachable. NDP is used by both hosts and routers, and its functions include Address Resolution, Duplicate Address Detection, Neighbor Unreachability Detection and Redirection. If it is not secured, it is vulnerable to various attacks.

The original NDP specifications called for IPsec to protect NDP messages, but did not give detailed instructions. IPsec could only be used with manually configured security associations because of bootstrapping problems with IKE, and the number of associations needed can be very large. SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) takes a different route and does not use IPsec.

SEND is meant for links where physical security is not assured, such as wireless. Using identity certificates on end hosts to authorize addresses, and securing proxy ND, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Normally, anyone on the local network can shout 'I am the router!' and be believed. SEND is a way to check ID before believing anyone.

sections.title: How SEND Fits Together
sections.content:
NDP messages follow the ICMPv6 format: an ICMPv6 header, message-specific data, and zero or more options in Type-Length-Value form. SEND leaves the base messages alone (Router Solicitation and Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, Redirect) and secures them with new options. The RFC lists four ingredients:

  • Certification paths anchored on a trust anchor, to show that a router is authorized to act as a router.
  • Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs), so the sender of a message is the owner of the address it claims. The CGA format and procedures are in RFC 3972.
  • An RSA Signature option protecting all Neighbor and Router Discovery messages.
  • Timestamp and Nonce options to prevent replay attacks.

RSA is mandated on purpose: several signature algorithms would break compatibility or force implementers to support several. If a flaw were found in RSA, a stronger algorithm could be added and its signatures would take precedence, the way RSA-signed information takes precedence over unsigned information.
sections.eli5: SEND gives each message a signature, a proof that the sender owns its address, and a freshness stamp, like a letter with a seal, a return address you can check, and today's date.

sections.title: The CGA and RSA Signature Options
sections.content:
The CGA option (type 11) carries the CGA Parameters data structure, which includes the sender's public key, plus padding. Receivers check the claimed source address against those parameters first. That check is a cheap hash verification. Only if it succeeds does the receiver go on to the more expensive signature check, and even then nothing is trusted until the signature has been verified.

The RSA Signature option (type 12) holds a Key Hash and a Digital Signature. The Key Hash is the leftmost 128 bits of a SHA-1 hash of the sender's public key, tying the signature to a known key. The signature is a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature computed over a fixed 128-bit SEND type tag, the IPv6 source and destination addresses, the ICMP type, code and checksum, the NDP message header, and all options that come before the signature option. The signature option is therefore added as the last option, and receivers ignore any options after it.

A node configured for SEND MUST put the RSA Signature option in Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement, Router Advertisement and Redirect messages. Router Solicitations need it unless sent from the unspecified address. If a message contains both a CGA option and an RSA Signature option, the key in the CGA Parameters MUST be the one named by the Key Hash, or the packet is silently discarded.

Receivers can be configured per message type to require a trust anchor, a CGA, both, or either. The default minimum key length for CGA keys SHOULD be 1024 bits.
sections.eli5: The CGA option is like showing that your name is built from your fingerprint. The signature is you signing the whole message so nobody can change it on the way.

sections.title: Timestamps and Nonces Against Replay
sections.content:
An attacker could record a valid signed message and send it again. SEND uses two options to stop that. The Nonce option (type 14) covers solicitation and advertisement pairs: the sender of a solicitation includes a random number of at least 6 bytes, remembers it, and accepts only an advertisement that carries a copy. Together with the signatures this forms a challenge-response exchange.

The Timestamp option (type 13) covers unsolicited messages, which can go to multicast addresses where no earlier exchange exists. It is a 64-bit value counting seconds since January 1, 1970 UTC: 48 bits of whole seconds and 16 bits of 1/64K fractions of a second. Senders SHOULD set it from their real-time clock.

For each peer, a receiver SHOULD remember when it last accepted a SEND message and the timestamp in it. A message from a new peer is accepted if the timestamp is within a configured delta of the arrival time (default 300 seconds). For a known peer, the new timestamp is compared with the previous one, allowing a small fuzz factor (1 second) and clock drift (1 percent). A message with a valid signature but no Timestamp MUST be silently discarded.

Nodes SHOULD also limit the resources they spend on unsolicited messages, since each one forces an expensive signature check.
sections.eli5: A nonce is a secret word you ask the other person to repeat back, so you know their answer is for your question. A timestamp is the date on a letter, so an old letter cannot pass as new.

sections.title: Authorizing Routers with Certificates
sections.content:
Rogue routers are easy to set up on an unsecured link, and a newly connected host cannot reach off-link nodes to check one. SEND therefore requires routers to be authorized. Routers hold certificates issued from a trust anchor, and hosts are configured with the trust anchors they accept. A router's authorization says it may act as a router and, optionally, which subnet prefixes it may advertise. The RFC notes that no global root for this exists, and describes both a global and a decentralized deployment model.

Certificates are X.509v3 and SHOULD carry the X.509 extension for IP addresses (RFC 3779), so each certificate in a path lists prefixes that are a subset of its issuer's. Hosts MUST accept only RSA keys. The null prefix ::/0 means the router is allowed to advertise any prefix.

To avoid putting long certificate chains in Router Advertisements, SEND defines two ICMPv6 messages, Certification Path Solicitation (type 148) and Certification Path Advertisement (type 149). A host asks for a path to one of its trust anchors, and the router answers with certificates in separate components, starting with the certificate after the trust anchor and ending with the router's own. The trust anchor's certificate SHOULD NOT be sent. Both messages use hop limit 255.

Because a new host usually cannot do an online revocation check yet, it must treat acceptance as provisional and check as soon as it has connectivity. If that check fails or is disrupted, it SHOULD stop using the router as default. Hosts retry a solicitation with doubling intervals and give up after 15 seconds.
sections.eli5: A router shows a chain of letters: the trusted authority vouches for a company, and the company vouches for this router. The host only trusts the router if the chain starts with someone it already trusts.

sections.title: Mixing Secured and Unsecured Nodes
sections.content:
Links can contain both SEND and non-SEND nodes during a transition. Non-SEND nodes ignore the unknown options, so they treat secured messages like unsecured ones. SEND nodes SHOULD handle both kinds, but give priority to secured information. A message counts as secured only if it has a valid signature option.

Several rules keep attackers out of a mixed link. All solicitations and unsolicited advertisements from a SEND node MUST be secured. Neighbor Cache, Prefix List and Default Router List entries MUST carry a secured or unsecured flag, and unsecured messages MUST NOT change secured entries. A default router is chosen from unsecured routers only if no reachable SEND router exists. A SEND node SHOULD offer a setting to ignore all unsecured messages, to enforce SEND-only networks, with the default allowing both.

For Duplicate Address Detection with CGAs, a node generates a new address if a collision shows up, and gives up after three consecutive attempts. By default it accepts unsecured replies for the first tentative address but ignores them for the second and third.

By default a SEND node SHOULD use only CGAs for its own addresses. The RFC states that static addresses and addresses built from fixed interface identifiers are not protected by this specification.
sections.eli5: Some kids on the playground have ID badges and some do not. The teacher listens to the badge kids first, and does not let a kid without a badge replace what a badge kid said.

sections.title: What SEND Does and Does Not Protect
sections.content:
SEND counters the threats described in RFC 3756: spoofed Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, Neighbor Unreachability Detection failure, Duplicate Address Detection denial of service, and rogue Router Advertisements, plus replay attacks via the Nonce and Timestamp options.

It has clear limits. It provides no confidentiality for NDP, does not compensate for an unsecured link layer, and does not cryptographically bind a link-layer frame address to the IPv6 address. It does not protect against brute-force attacks on a router or a compromised router, and it does not stop the Neighbor Discovery DoS attack where a router is made to solicit nonexistent addresses. MLD, which nodes use to subscribe to multicast groups, has no security either.

SEND itself can be attacked: an attacker can send many packets that force expensive asymmetric verification. The CGA hash check before the signature check helps, and implementations SHOULD track resources spent on signature-bearing packets and start discarding selectively. The RFC also notes that CGAs have a 59-bit hash value, with the analysis left to RFC 3972. Replay attacks remain possible while a timestamp is still valid if a node has flushed its cached state, and attacks on time synchronization can widen that window.
sections.eli5: SEND checks ID cards, but it cannot stop someone from reading your mail, or from flooding you with so many ID cards to check that you get tired.

sections.title: Protocol Values and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA for two ICMPv6 types from the informational range: 148 for Certification Path Solicitation and 149 for Certification Path Advertisement. It also asks for six Neighbor Discovery option types: CGA (11), RSA Signature (12), Timestamp (13), Nonce (14), Trust Anchor (15) and Certificate (16).

It creates a new 128-bit value in the CGA Message Type namespace, and two new name spaces: Name Type in the Trust Anchor option (1 is a DER encoded X.501 Name, 2 is an FQDN) and Cert Type in the Certificate option (1 is an X.509v3 certificate). New values in both can be assigned by Standards Action.

Section 10 lists the constants. Hosts use CPS_RETRY of 1 second, CPS_RETRY_FRAGMENTS of 2 seconds and CPS_RETRY_MAX of 15 seconds. Routers SHOULD NOT send more than MAX_CPA_RATE, 10 per second. The timestamp variables are TIMESTAMP_DELTA of 300 seconds, TIMESTAMP_FUZZ of 1 second and TIMESTAMP_DRIFT of 1 percent.
sections.eli5: This part asks the official number keeper for new numbers, like asking the school to give each new club its own room number.

viz.caption: NEW NEIGHBOR DISCOVERY OPTION TYPES (RFC 3971, SECTION 11)

items.label: CGA
items.desc: Carries the CGA Parameters so the sender's address can be verified.

items.label: RSA Signature
items.desc: Key Hash plus a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature over the message.

items.label: Nonce
items.desc: Links an advertisement to the solicitation that triggered it.

items.label: Trust Anchor
items.desc: Names a trust anchor the host accepts.

items.label: Certificate
items.desc: Carries one X.509v3 certificate of a certification path.
